The first time I visited Kamal's clinic, I watched him with a crying child: kneeling, voice soft, making up a story about a brave elephant. Three patients later he was still smiling. I was so proud.
Then he came home at nine and I asked about his day, and he said, "Fine." I asked if he wanted dal or khichdi, and he said, "Whatever. Doesn't matter." He scrolled on his phone through dinner. For months I thought he had simply stopped caring about me.
One night I said so, gently. He put the phone down and looked stricken. "I use it all up," he said. "By the time I get home there's nothing left."
We agreed on a small thing: twenty minutes alone on the balcony when he gets in, then real time together. Some nights I, Arohi, get the soft voice now too.

qa.a: A story about a brave elephant.

What I've noticed about Francis over the last month:
- At work events he is warm, funny and patient. His customers at the bank adore him. Last Friday I watched him listen to an old man's complaint for twenty minutes without once checking his watch.
- At home he walks in, says "hi" and goes straight to the shower. At dinner, if I ask a question, he says, "Can we not?" On Sunday he snapped when I asked about the electricity bill.

What I'd like to try: one work-free evening a week, and him telling me when he's drained instead of snapping.

Tuesday
Went to pick Manjula up from school today and watched from the gate. Forty Class 2 kids around her, and she was laughing, crouching to tie laces, praising a wobbly drawing as if it were a masterpiece. A parent stopped me: "Your wife is a saint." I agreed.
At home she dropped her bag, said, "Please don't talk to me for a bit," and lay on the sofa with her eyes shut. When I asked what she wanted for dinner, she said, "I don't care, Devika, anything." It stung. It always stings.
But I've started to see it: she isn't cold to me. She's spent. Every drop of patience goes to those forty kids. I get the empty cup.
Tomorrow I'll ask her: can we have Sunday mornings where nobody needs anything from her, and then a proper walk, just us? I miss the laughing version.
Devika

On Sunday she said, gently, "The farmers get your best hours. Could we have one of them? Maybe Sunday morning, a walk to the lake, before your phone starts?"

Hemant,

I'm writing this because when I try to say it at night, we're both too tired.

Yesterday I heard you on the phone with that difficult supplier. You were so patient. You listened to him for forty minutes, you made a joke, you calmed him right down. I remember falling in love with that voice.

I'm not angry. I miss you. Could we try something, maybe a short walk before your last calls, or one evening a week with phones off?

Irawati
